title: Redis: the basics
seriesDescription: How to use Redis in system design interviews: the data model, durability limits, clustering, caching, distributed locks, leaderboards, rate limiting, geo search, streams and pub/sub, with the trade-offs interviewers probe.
description: What Redis is, why one thread makes it fast and predictable, its data structures, how commands look and how fast it really is.
source: Study notes: how to use Redis in system design interviews

options.text: A key-value store whose values are data structures such as hashes and sorted sets.
options.why: Right: every object is a value stored at a string key.

options.text: A relational store with tables, rows and a query planner.
options.why: Redis has no tables, joins or planner; that is deliberate.

options.text: A document database that indexes every field of every value.
options.why: Values are not indexed by field; you reach data through its key.

options.text: A column store that keeps each attribute in its own file.
options.why: Redis keeps data in memory as keyed data structures.

questions.explanation: Keys are strings and the value is where the data structure lives. The way you choose keys is the way you organise and scale the data.

questions.prompt: Why is Redis's one-command-at-a-time execution a feature rather than a limit?

options.text: Command execution never needs locks, and simple commands finish in microseconds.
options.why: Right: atomicity comes for free and one core is rarely the bottleneck.

options.text: It lets Redis use every CPU core at once for a single command.
options.why: The point is the opposite: commands run one after another.

options.text: It guarantees every write reaches disk before the reply is sent.
options.why: Durability depends on persistence settings, not on threading.

options.text: It removes the need for any network protocol between client and server.
options.why: Clients still talk to Redis over a wire protocol (RESP).

questions.explanation: Think "one command at a time, in order". That is why a Lua script or a single command is atomic and easy to reason about.

questions.prompt: Select all the data structures Redis supports out of the box.

options.text: Sorted sets, usable as priority queues and leaderboards.
options.why: Yes: scored members kept in rank order.

options.text: Streams, which are append-only logs.
options.why: Yes: the basis for work queues and event logs.

options.text: Geospatial indexes for proximity search.
options.why: Yes: GEOADD and GEOSEARCH are built in.

options.text: Relational tables with foreign keys and joins.
options.why: No: Redis has no relational model.

questions.explanation: Hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams and geo indexes cover most interview needs. Redis 8 adds JSON, Bloom filters and time series.

questions.prompt: What does the sequence SET foo 1, then INCR foo return from INCR?

options.text: 2, the incremented value.
options.why: Right: INCR atomically adds one and returns the result.

options.text: 1, the original value.
options.why: INCR returns the new value, not the old one.

options.text: An error, because strings cannot be incremented.
options.why: A string holding an integer can be incremented.

options.text: OK, and the value is changed later in the background.
options.why: The change and reply happen immediately.

questions.explanation: Redis commands read like their data structure analogues, which makes them easy to reason about.

questions.prompt: Roughly what can one Redis node do?

options.text: About 100k writes per second, with sub-millisecond reads over the network.
options.why: Right: a handy interview-level figure.

options.text: About 100 writes per second, because it fsyncs every one in a typical production setup.
options.why: That is far too low; it keeps data in memory.

options.text: Millions of complex multi-table joins per second for most everyday workloads.
options.why: Redis has no joins.

options.text: The speed depends only on how many keys exist.
options.why: Command cost and network round trips matter more than key count.

questions.explanation: Speed comes from being in-memory. It makes some anti-patterns affordable, such as many tiny commands, especially when pipelined.

questions.prompt: You must fetch 100 cached items. What is the best way to do that against Redis?

options.text: Pipeline the commands or use MGET so one round trip serves all of them.
options.why: Right: the server cost is tiny; round trips are what add up.

options.text: Fetch each item one by one, since Redis is too fast to matter under normal operating conditions.
options.why: It works, but 100 round trips are avoidable latency.

options.text: Copy all 100 items into a single huge string value first as a general rule of thumb.
options.why: That is awkward and loses per-item expiry.

options.text: Use a SQL join between the keys.
options.why: Redis has no joins.

questions.explanation: N+1 against Redis will not sink a design, but pipelining or MGET still pays one round trip instead of a hundred.

questions.prompt: True or false: Redis is fast mainly because it keeps its data in memory.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: speed is a function of its in-memory design.

options.text: False
options.why: It is the in-memory design that gives it the speed.

questions.explanation: Memory access is far cheaper than disk. The price is cost per gigabyte and weaker default durability.

questions.prompt: Why do interviewers like Redis answers that stay close to simple data structures?

options.text: Scaling consequences are easy to reason about without knowing Redis internals.
options.why: Right: you can go deep without trivia.

options.text: Redis hides all distribution details so nothing needs discussing in the majority of deployments.
options.why: You still must reason about keys, slots and failures.

options.text: Redis chooses the best data structure for you automatically without any extra configuration.
options.why: You pick the structure and design the key.

options.text: Simple structures cannot fail, so there is nothing to probe.
options.why: Interviewers probe durability, hot keys and clustering.

questions.explanation: Redis is deliberately simple: no optimisers or query planners, just fast operations on known structures.
